Nepal death toll crosses 1,000 as rescuers race to find workers trapped in mud-filled tunnels
- Published
The death toll in Nepal from devastating floods on the border with Tibet has crossed 1,000, according to the country's disaster agency.
More than 3,900 people remain missing - of whom more than 600 are workers believed to be trapped in a vast network of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower sites along Trishuli River.
Engineers have been pumping air into the tunnels - and while a team did manage to gain entry to one of them, it withdrew after finding no-one there.
"I wish we could find him. I wish he would come home," Anushila Bhandari, wife of Aurus Bhandari, a 33-year-old engineer missing on a project site, told BBC Nepali.
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Monday that 279 people had been rescued from the sites.
The rescue operation is being spearheaded by an international team made up of Chinese and Nepalese military personnel, while experts from India, Korea and Australia are also involved.
"I still have a 50% hope that he is alive because there is an oxygen system inside," Sita Pandey, whose husband was working in the plant when the floods hit, told Nepalese daily Kantipur.
Nepal relies heavily on hydropower and has spent years developing the projects along its mountainous river systems. At least 11 projects either completed or under construction were damaged in the floods, authorities said.
Rescuers began pumping air into a tunnel over the weekend, but the families of those trapped say that should have been done earlier.
A team was able to get into a tunnel leading to one hydropower plant earlier on Monday, but retreated after no one was found there.
"The longer it takes, the more our hope dies. This operation must move much faster because every second is meaningful to us," Jiban Khadka, whose relative is also trapped inside the plant, told Kantipur.
"It's a frustratingly slow operation," Khadka added.
Rescue operations had been "intensified", Nepalese leader Shah said, noting that the floods were "not an ordinary" event.
"This incident indicates that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change.
"It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change," Shah wrote in a Facebook post late on Monday.

corpus.signal_text:
More than 1,000 dead from catastrophic Nepal-China floods as rescuers search for survivors
Thousands still missing, including hundreds believed trapped in tunnels
The death toll from catastrophic flooding in Nepal and China passed 1,000 on Tuesday, authorities said, as rescue teams worked to reach communities cut off by the disaster.
Nepal's disaster agency said Tuesday that 987 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreigners. Chinese authorities, in their latest update on Sunday, reported 16 deaths and 546 people still missing.
At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepalese authorities. Emergency crews have been using helicopters and other aircraft to reach stranded communities in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed by the flooding and landslides.
The disaster began Wednesday with a chain of events high in the Himalayas. A glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.
Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appears to have involved the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier in the Himalayan region. The rockfall was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
The resulting surge of water and debris entered rivers that flow through valleys in Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly. Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges and carried mud and rocks downstream.
Authorities are still searching for thousands of people who remain unaccounted for on Tuesday. Rescue teams are also working to provide assistance to survivors in areas where roads and other transportation routes have been damaged or cut off.
- Rescuers search for thousands following deadly Nepal-China flood
- Hundreds feared stuck in hydropower tunnels in Nepal
For rescuers, the immediate priority remains finding at least 900 workers who are missing from 12 hydropower projects damaged by the flash floods, about 500 of whom are believed to be trapped inside tunnels.
Visuals released by Nepal's army showed rescue teams entering dark, debris-filled tunnels, wading through mud and water and climbing over rocks as they searched for signs of life.
Bimal Sharma, a helicopter pilot who has been flying rescue missions since the disaster began, said he was shocked to see the devastation in Timure, a border town close to Tibet that he has known for years.

corpus.title: Nepal flood: Death toll tops 1,000 as rescue continues
corpus.signal_text:
Nepal flood: Death toll tops 1,000 as rescue continues
September 1, 2026
Nepalese authorities say 4,000 people remain unaccounted for as rescue teams with search dogs comb through mud, rocks and debris.
The death toll after a massive flash flood last week at the Himalayan border between Nepal and China has risen more than 1,000 people, local authorities said on Tuesday.
In Nepal, 987 deaths have already been reported, with almost 4,000 people still being unaccounted for. In China,16 deaths and 546 missing people have been reported.
The list of missing people includes some 800 foreign nationals.
Search and rescue teams are still carrying out operations despite difficult conditions and unstable terrain.
Search dogs are also taking part in the search efforts through mud, rocks and debris the flash floods left behind.
Roads were destroyed in places, cutting off access.
Efforts are also being made to locate the some 500 workers believed to be trapped inside the tunnels of twelve hydropower project tunnels, according to Nepalese authorities.
Climate change raises risk for region, PM says
The flash floods on August 28, started as a glacial collapse in the Himalayas triggered a powerful stream of rock, ice and meltwater into the valleys below.
The stream was so powerful that a seismic event of 5.2 magnitude was recorded.
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah reacted to the disaster by emphasizing the need to fight climate change.
"This incident has indicated that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing with climate change," he posted on social media.
"Therefore, this region must be alert, and at the same time, it is time for us to strongly raise the issue of disasters caused by climate change before the international community."
Edited by: Wesley Rahn

Roughly 80 Americans remain unaccounted for following the catastrophic Himalayan flood last Wednesday that killed hundreds of people, the State Department said.
The update marks a decrease from a previous estimate of at least 90 Americans who went missing near the Nepal-China border.
"We can confirm that 13 American citizens have made their way to safety in Nepal," a State Department spokesperson told Fox News.
Meanwhile, Nepal’s death toll has risen to 903, while the number of people still unaccounted for has nearly doubled to roughly 4,200, according to an update from local officials Sunday.
TRAPPED NEPALI WORKERS PULLED FROM HYDROPOWER TUNNEL AFTER CATASTROPHIC FLOODING
According to officials, the disaster occurred in north-central Nepal when a distant slope failure involving a glacier triggered a rapidly moving debris flow that traveled roughly 62 miles downstream before striking a populated area. Footage from the disaster showed a massive surge of water and debris suddenly rushing through the valleys, engulfing buildings in its path.
On Sunday, a spokesperson for Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs provided an update on the toll.
"So far, 903 bodies have been recovered from the areas and about 4200 people are still unaccounted for. Over 10,000 people have been rescued from the regions, including over 323 foreign nationals. As per the available data, about 590 foreign nationals are still missing, from 39 countries," the spokesperson said.
Twenty-two of the missing Americans were part of a pilgrimage affiliated with a Tennessee-based nonprofit group, Isha Foundation coordination leader Jyoti Jankowski told Fox News Saturday. They were inside an immigration building when the flooding struck the area, Jankowski said.
Authorities said Nepal is coordinating with neighboring countries and the international community to provide relief, with supplies already arriving from countries including India and China.
More supplies are expected to arrive from the U.S., United Arab Emirates, Myanmar, Qatar, the U.K., Australia, the Republic of Korea, Japan, New Zealand, Malaysia, Singapore, Bangladesh, Pakistan and other international organizations, officials said.
"Relief and humanitarian assistance are being provided in the affected areas. We are deeply grateful to our friends and partners for their solidarity, goodwill and generous offers of support at this difficult time," the spokesperson said.

Nearly 4,500 people are missing after the gigantic wave of freezing water, rocks and debris from a high-altitude glacial collapse roared downstream on Wednesday, wiping out entire settlements and gouging a path of destruction through Nepal.
Nepali rescue teams are digging, drilling and blasting through debris in a race against time in treacherous conditions to free around 100 hydropower workers believed trapped in multiple tunnels.
So far, only corpses have been pulled out of tunnels blocked with sludge.
“We are focused on search and rescue efforts at the tunnels, our work is continuing,” Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal Army spokesman, told AFP on Tuesday.
“Our soldiers are also deployed to collect bodies and prevent the spread of disease.”

In the capital Kathmandu, crowds lined up to search for their missing relatives, posting photographs on a long wall outside a hospital, in the fading hope of finding them alive.
Debu Sapkota, a 58-year-old driver, came to post photos of his 83-year-old mother-in-law and granddaughter who went missing in the town of Trishuli Bazaar, after being swept away by last week’s surge.
A warning alert sounded, but the elderly woman was “too old to run”, he recounts.
“Her granddaughter was helping her escape but both were swept away.”
Sapkota says he no longer has “any hope that they survived”, after witnesses saw them being carried away by the torrent.
“I am here hoping to find their bodies,” he said, holding up photos of the two missing women dressed in traditional clothes.

1,003 bodies recovered in Nepal floods; 4,000 still missing as rescue ops continue
As rescue teams battle rain and fresh alerts, Kathmandu is linking the disaster to climate change and seeking compensation from major emitters.
Nepal is battling the aftermath of catastrophic flash floods that have killed more than 1,000 people, left thousands missing and caused widespread destruction across the country.
The disaster was triggered after a collapse or avalanche of ice and rock near the Nepal-Tibet border sent a massive surge of water down the Bhotekoshi River, sweeping through settlements and damaging roads, bridges and hydropower projects.
Rescue operations are continuing on a massive scale, but intermittent rainfall and warnings of fresh floods have complicated efforts to reach affected areas.
DEATH TOLL CROSSES 1,000, THOUSANDS MISSING
The death toll has risen to 1,003 as security forces recover more bodies across eight affected districts.
Chitwan has reported the highest toll at 321, followed by Nawalparasi East with 216 deaths.
Around 4,000 people, including 583 foreign nationals, remain missing, raising fears that the toll could climb further. Nearly 12,000 people have been rescued so far.
The Nepalese government has deployed more than 21,300 security personnel for search, rescue and relief operations.
Helicopters are making repeated sorties to evacuate people stranded in inaccessible areas and deliver food and other essential supplies to communities cut off by the floods.
FRESH FLOOD THREAT KEEPS NEPAL ON ALERT
Even as rescue teams search for survivors, Nepal faces the threat of further flooding.
Authorities have issued fresh warnings across parts of eastern, central and western Nepal amid intermittent rainfall and rising river levels.
Rasuwa and Nuwakot are among the areas facing heightened risks, while alerts have been issued for several other districts.
Energy Minister Biraj Bhakta Shrestha on Tuesday held discussions with officials from the energy and meteorology departments and other experts to assess weather conditions and possible flood risks in Rasuwa, Nuwakot and other affected areas.
The government is now focusing on continuous river monitoring, improving early warning systems and speeding up measures to reduce the risk of another disaster.
Authorities are also working to install monitoring cameras and satellite-based communication systems in vulnerable areas.

corpus.title: Satellite images show how the Nepal flood disaster unfolded
corpus.signal_text:
On August 26 a glacier collapsed in the Langtang region of Nepal near the China border, triggering an ice and rock avalanche. This apparently entered the Lhende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river, where it either caused or contributed to a temporary blockage. When this burst, a catastrophic flash flood travelled almost 100 kilometres downstream.
A glacier collapses
There’s nothing to stop the avalanche down the Trishuli river valley
Did warm conditions play a role?
There is increasing interest in the role of unusually warm conditions and glacial permafrost instability. Warming can increase meltwater penetration into the crevasses of glaciers and weaken ice-rock bonds. British Antarctic Survey researchers reported unusually high ground temperatures two days before the collapse.

corpus.title: Nepal flash floods aftermath LIVE: Death toll surges to 1,003; nearly 4,000 still missing
corpus.signal_text:
The death toll from the deadly Himalayan flood in Nepal surged to 1,003 on Tuesday (September 1, 2026), with security forces recovering more bodies from eight districts of the country, officials said.
ALSO READ | Nepal disaster, a grim reminder to rethink preparedness | Data
Around 4,000 people remain missing, while nearly 12,000 have been rescued, the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said.
Flash floods, triggered by a collapse or avalanche of ice and rock near the Nepal-Tibet border, devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal on August 26. The Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.
ALSO READ | The Bhotekoshi flood | A Himalayan tragedy
As many as 321 bodies were recovered in Chitwan district, followed by 216 in Nawalparasi East, 170 in Nawalparasi West, 95 in Nuwakot, 65 in Gorkha, 57 in Dhading, 41 in Rasuwa and 38 in Tanahun, according to NDRRMA.
